pubis.name: Body of pubis and inferior pubic ramus

femur-lateral.name: Greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera

femur-medial.name: Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera

femur-shaft.name: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft

lateral-femoral-condyle.name: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle

above-medial-condyle.name: Posterior femur above the medial condyle

lateral-condyle-posterior.name: Posterolateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle

medial-tibial-condyle.name: Posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle

posterior-tibia.name: Posterior tibia above the soleal line

femoral.name: Femoral nerve
femoral.injury: Weak knee extension, so the knee may buckle when standing or climbing stairs. The patellar reflex is reduced or lost. Hip flexion is also weakened.
femoral.outsideRegion: Also supplies iliacus and pectineus, which arrive with the hip region.

obturator.name: Obturator nerve
obturator.injury: Weak hip adduction. The leg may swing outward when walking.
obturator.outsideRegion: Also supplies the adductor group and obturator externus, which arrive with the hip region.

sciatic.name: Sciatic nerve
sciatic.injury: Weak knee flexion and hip extension from loss of the hamstrings, plus loss of every muscle below the knee, including foot drop.
sciatic.outsideRegion: Divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves, usually just above the knee.

tibial.name: Tibial nerve
tibial.injury: In the thigh (tibial division): weak hamstrings. Below the knee: weak plantarflexion, so pushing off and rising onto the toes become difficult.
tibial.outsideRegion: Also supplies soleus and the deep calf muscles, which arrive with the leg region.

common-fibular.name: Common fibular nerve
common-fibular.injury: Foot drop: the foot cannot be pulled up (dorsiflexed) or turned out (everted). It wraps around the neck of the fibula, where it is easily injured.
common-fibular.outsideRegion: Supplies the anterior and lateral leg muscles, which arrive with the leg region.

hip-flexion.name: Hip flexion
hip-flexion.note: Iliopsoas, the main hip flexor, arrives with the hip region.

hip-extension.name: Hip extension
hip-extension.note: Gluteus maximus, the other main hip extensor, arrives with the hip region.

hip-abduction.name: Hip abduction
hip-abduction.note: Gluteus medius and minimus, the main abductors, arrive with the hip region.

hip-adduction.name: Hip adduction
hip-adduction.note: The adductor group, the main adductors, arrives with the hip region.

hip-lateral-rotation.name: Hip lateral rotation
hip-lateral-rotation.note: Not animated yet. The deep gluteal muscles, the main lateral rotators, arrive with the hip region.

tibial-medial-rotation.name: Medial rotation of the tibia
tibial-medial-rotation.note: Not animated yet. Only possible with the knee bent.

tibial-lateral-rotation.name: Lateral rotation of the tibia
tibial-lateral-rotation.note: Not animated yet. Only possible with the knee bent.

knee-unlocking.name: Unlocking the extended knee
knee-unlocking.note: Popliteus rotates the femur laterally on the planted tibia to start flexion from full extension. The rotation itself is not animated yet.

ankle-plantarflexion.name: Ankle plantarflexion
ankle-plantarflexion.note: Not animated yet. Soleus, the other half of the calcaneal tendon, arrives with the leg region.

rectus-femoris.name: Rectus femoris
rectus-femoris.originText: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head) and the ilium just above the acetabulum (reflected head).
rectus-femoris.insertionText: Base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
rectus-femoris.note: The only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip, so it is a two-joint muscle.

vastus-lateralis.name: Vastus lateralis
vastus-lateralis.originText: Greater trochanter, upper intertrochanteric line and the lateral lip of the linea aspera.
vastus-lateralis.insertionText: Base and lateral border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
vastus-lateralis.note: The largest part of the quadriceps.

vastus-medialis.name: Vastus medialis
vastus-medialis.originText: Intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera.
vastus-medialis.insertionText: Base and medial border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
vastus-medialis.note: Its lowest fibres (often called VMO) pull the patella medially and help it track in the femoral groove.

vastus-intermedius.name: Vastus intermedius
vastus-intermedius.originText: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft.
vastus-intermedius.insertionText: Base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
vastus-intermedius.note: Lies deep to rectus femoris, directly on the femur.

sartorius.name: Sartorius
sartorius.insertionText: Upper medial surface of the tibia, as part of the pes anserinus.
sartorius.note: The longest muscle in the body. Its combined actions put the leg in the cross-legged sitting position.

gracilis.name: Gracilis
gracilis.originText: Body of the pubis and the inferior pubic ramus.
gracilis.insertionText: Upper medial surface of the tibia, as part of the pes anserinus.
gracilis.note: The only adductor that crosses the knee.

semitendinosus.name: Semitendinosus
semitendinosus.insertionText: Upper medial surface of the tibia, as part of the pes anserinus.
semitendinosus.nerveNote: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
semitendinosus.note: Its long tendon makes up the lower half of the muscle.

semimembranosus.name: Semimembranosus
semimembranosus.insertionText: Posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle.
semimembranosus.nerveNote: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
semimembranosus.note: Lies deep to semitendinosus. Its flat upper tendon gives it its name.

biceps-femoris-long.name: Biceps femoris, long head
biceps-femoris-long.insertionText: Lateral side of the head of the fibula.
biceps-femoris-long.nerveNote: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve

biceps-femoris-short.name: Biceps femoris, short head
biceps-femoris-short.originText: Lateral lip of the linea aspera and the lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
biceps-femoris-short.insertionText: Lateral side of the head of the fibula, shared with the long head.
biceps-femoris-short.nerveNote: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve
biceps-femoris-short.note: The only hamstring part that does not cross the hip and is not supplied by the tibial division. A classic exam question.

popliteus.name: Popliteus
popliteus.originText: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, with attachment to the lateral meniscus.
popliteus.insertionText: Posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line.
popliteus.note: Called the key that unlocks the knee.

gastrocnemius-medial.name: Gastrocnemius, medial head
gastrocnemius-medial.originText: Posterior surface of the femur just above the medial condyle.
gastrocnemius-medial.insertionText: Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
gastrocnemius-medial.note: Crosses both the knee and the ankle, so it plantarflexes best with the knee straight.

gastrocnemius-lateral.name: Gastrocnemius, lateral head
gastrocnemius-lateral.originText: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle.
gastrocnemius-lateral.insertionText: Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
gastrocnemius-lateral.note: Crosses both the knee and the ankle, so it plantarflexes best with the knee straight.

acl.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
acl.attachmentText: Anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, running up and back to the inner (medial) surface of the lateral femoral condyle.
acl.function: Stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and limits hyperextension.
acl.tautText: Tight in full extension. Its anteromedial band stays fairly tight as the knee bends.

pcl.name: Posterior cruciate ligament
pcl.attachmentText: Posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, running up and forward to the outer (lateral) surface of the medial femoral condyle.
pcl.function: Stops the tibia sliding backward on the femur. Stronger than the ACL.
pcl.tautText: Tightens as the knee bends; tightest in flexion.

mcl.name: Tibial collateral ligament
mcl.mesh: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament.r
extraMeshes: Deep part of tibial collateral ligament.r
mcl.attachmentText: Medial epicondyle of the femur to the medial condyle and upper medial shaft of the tibia. Its deep fibres attach to the medial meniscus.
mcl.function: Resists valgus stress (the knee being pushed inward).
mcl.tautText: Tight in full extension; slackens as the knee bends.

lcl.name: Fibular collateral ligament
lcl.attachmentText: Lateral epicondyle of the femur to the lateral surface of the head of the fibula. It is cord-like and stands clear of the joint capsule and the lateral meniscus.
lcl.function: Resists varus stress (the knee being pushed outward).
lcl.tautText: Tight in full extension; slackens as the knee bends.

patellar-ligament.name: Patellar ligament
patellar-ligament.attachmentText: Apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity.
patellar-ligament.function: Carries the pull of the quadriceps from the patella to the tibia. It is really the continuation of the quadriceps tendon.
patellar-ligament.tautText: Under load whenever the quadriceps contracts; stretched further as the knee bends.

medial-meniscus.name: Medial meniscus
medial-meniscus.text: C-shaped fibrocartilage pad on the medial tibial plateau. Firmly attached to the deep part of the MCL, so it moves less and is torn more often than the lateral meniscus.

lateral-meniscus.name: Lateral meniscus
lateral-meniscus.text: Nearly circular fibrocartilage pad on the lateral tibial plateau. Not attached to the LCL, so it is more mobile than the medial meniscus.

glossary.origin: Where a muscle attaches to the bone that stays relatively still.
glossary.insertion: Where a muscle attaches to the bone it moves.
glossary.innervation: The nerve that controls a muscle, with the spinal cord levels (roots) its fibres come from.
glossary.action: The movement a muscle produces when it pulls its insertion toward its origin.
glossary.prime mover: The muscle that does most of the work in a movement.
glossary.two-joint muscle: A muscle that crosses two joints and acts on both, like rectus femoris or the hamstrings.
glossary.flexion: Bending a joint so the angle between the bones gets smaller.
glossary.extension: Straightening a joint so the angle between the bones gets larger.
glossary.abduction: Moving a limb away from the midline of the body.
glossary.adduction: Moving a limb toward the midline of the body.
glossary.plantarflexion: Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe.
glossary.condyle: A rounded knob at the end of a bone that forms part of a joint.
glossary.epicondyle: A bump on the side of a condyle where ligaments and muscles attach.
glossary.tuberosity: A large, rough raised area where a tendon attaches.
glossary.linea aspera: The vertical ridge on the back of the femur shaft where several thigh muscles attach.
glossary.pes anserinus: The shared insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the upper medial tibia. Latin for goose's foot.
glossary.taut: Stretched tight, so the ligament is resisting motion.
glossary.valgus: A force or position that pushes the knee inward (toward the other knee).
glossary.varus: A force or position that pushes the knee outward.
glossary.roots: The spinal nerve levels (for example L2–L4) whose fibres make up a nerve.
glossary.intercondylar area: The space between the two condyles of the tibia, where the cruciate ligaments attach.
glossary.acetabulum: The socket of the hip bone that holds the head of the femur.

knee-joint.name: Knee ligaments
knee-joint.summary: The ligaments that hold the femur and tibia together, and the menisci that sit between them.
